newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Black market, drugs flourish in south Albania.
newsitem.headline: Black market, drugs flourish in south Albania.

text.p: Albania's black market and drug trade looks set for a boom in the rebel-held south with dozens of armed gangs roaming near the border with Greece and Albanian security forces long gone.
"I'll show you how most of us make our living. I'll take you to my hashish field," said Ahmet, who now works as a taxi driver for foreign reporters in this southern port.

With a Kalashnikov by his side and a bullet hole in the windshield he drove his old Mercedes past two tanks guarding Sarande's northern entrance and then off to a dirt-road towards the mountains which led to a hashish plantation.

Ahmet's wife and brother were busy on Thursday watering about 100 plants with buckets from a nearby spring. Inside a wooden warehouse at the edge of the field, there were about 15 huge sacks packed with hashish ready for export.

"When the sea is calm we take them by speed-boat to Italy and Greece. We make at least one trip a week with more than 60 kilos (170 pounds). We meet Greek and Italian dealers at the coast and they pay good cash in drachmas or dollars," Ahmed said.
Hashish growth in southern Albania began four years ago when Greeks and Italians gave locals seeds. An estimated 80,000 people in southern Albania are involved in hashish plantations.
Ahmet's crop was one of many in the mountains outside Sarande. A number of fields belong to his friends, mostly couples in their thirties.

"We had no problems with police -- and now with the rebels -- in growing hashish," said Irene, Ahmet's wife. "They know it is the only way to make a living if you don't have a relative in Greece or Italy to send you money. There is no work here."

Sarande, just across from the Greek holiday island of Corfu, has some summer tourism from passing yachts but otherwise there is little economic activity. It was the second town to fall to the rebels after Vlore two weeks ago.
Locals are now all armed with Kalashnikovs.
The main Kakavia border crossing with Greece was abandoned by Albanian security forces last week and travellers are now often at the mercy of armed gangs in pickup trucks.
Rebel councils in Sarande and Gjirokaster, the other major southern town, have managed to restore some order but there is little they can do to control gangs outside the towns.

"I make about $12,000 everytime a truck with petrol makes it across Kakavia. We pay no customs because there is nobody at the Albanian customs booth. But then these punks may stop you and take all the gas and the truck," said Niko, who runs a chain of five gas stations.
Electrical appliances from Greece, chocolate, alcoholic beverages, flour, and medicine were also hot items on the black market list. All cigarettes, sold by street vendors, are marked tax free.
Masked gangs around Kakavia often stop motorists at gunpoint and steal their gas and goods. One man was shot dead on Tuesday a few metres (yards) from the border for refusing to hand over his money.

"I gave some blood for a friend being operated on and the doctor said I had to pay $5 for the syringe. The syringes came the other day as part of Greek aid and the doctor was selling them," said Aristo Curpe, a Sarande resident.

A Greek minesweeper with food and medical supplies waited outside Sarande's port for three hours before docking on Thursday as rebel leaders met with Greek consul in Gjirokaster Nikos Kanellos, to arrange distribution and prevent a looting.
